questions.question: A company runs a database on an EC2 instance in us-east-1a. A new analytics instance is launched in us-east-1b and must use the same data. What is the correct approach?
options: Detach the volume and attach it to the instance in us-east-1b
Take a snapshot of the volume and restore it as a new volume in us-east-1b
Create a new empty volume in us-east-1b and copy files over the network
Enable Delete on Termination on the volume so it can be recreated in us-east-1b
questions.explanation: An EBS volume is locked to its Availability Zone, so the only supported way to move data across AZs is to snapshot it and restore the snapshot as a new volume in the target AZ. Detaching and re-attaching keeps the volume in us-east-1a and it cannot attach in us-east-1b; a new empty volume plus network copy is not the standard mechanism and adds avoidable work; Delete on Termination controls deletion at instance termination and has nothing to do with AZ placement.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an EBS volume?
options: A physical disk that is part of the host running the instance
A network drive attached to an instance that persists data after termination
An object store bucket mountable by many instances simultaneously
A local buffer that is erased whenever the instance stops
questions.explanation: EBS is a network drive ('network USB stick') attached to an instance over the network, and it persists data even after the instance terminates. It is not a physical drive on the host; S3 is the object store, and EBS is block storage bound to one instance at a time at the foundational level; it is not an ephemeral local buffer.

questions.question: A team provisioned a 1 TB EBS volume with high provisioned IOPS but the application only fills 200 GB and rarely drives IOPS. How is billing calculated?
options: For the 200 GB actually stored and the IOPS actually consumed
For the full provisioned size and provisioned IOPS
For provisioned size only, with IOPS included at no charge
For used capacity only, since an unattached volume is free
questions.explanation: EBS bills all provisioned capacity — both provisioned GB and provisioned IOPS — regardless of actual use, so over-provisioning costs money even when idle. Billing is not based on stored data or consumed IOPS; IOPS are not free with a volume; and an unattached or lightly used volume is still billed for its provisioned capacity.

questions.question: A web server instance is terminated and the team notices that its root volume disappeared while a separately attached data volume remained. Which behaviour explains this?
options: The root volume had Delete on Termination enabled by default; the data volume had it disabled by default
All attached volumes are deleted on termination unless they are re-attached within an hour
The data volume survived only because it was larger than the root volume
Volumes survive termination only if an EBS snapshot was taken in the last 24 hours
questions.explanation: Delete on Termination is enabled by default on the root volume (so it is deleted) and disabled by default on other attached volumes (so they persist); the attribute can be changed via the console or AWS CLI. There is no re-attach grace period; volume size does not determine deletion; and snapshots do not change the termination behaviour of a volume.

questions.question: An architect must keep the root volume of an EC2 instance after the instance is terminated. What is the recommended action?
options: Copy the root volume to a snapshot before each boot
Disable the Delete on Termination attribute on the root volume
Attach the root volume to a second instance as a data volume
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the root volume's snapshot
questions.explanation: Delete on Termination is a per-volume attribute, and disabling it on the root volume is the documented use case for preserving the root volume when the instance terminates. Snapshotting before each boot is unnecessary overhead and not a guarantee of preservation; a root volume cannot simply be attached as a data volume of another instance; FSR reduces first-use restore latency and does not affect termination.

questions.question: A company needs a long-term backup of a rarely restored EBS volume and wants the lowest storage cost, accepting that recovery may take a day or more. Which option fits?
options: Keep a standard EBS snapshot in the Region
Move the snapshot to EBS Snapshot Archive
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot
Configure a Recycle Bin rule for deleted snapshots
questions.explanation: EBS Snapshot Archive moves the snapshot to an archive tier that is 75% cheaper, at the cost of a restore time of within 24 to 72 hours — acceptable when speed is not required. A standard snapshot costs more to keep; FSR removes first-use latency and costs extra, the opposite of cost saving; Recycle Bin retains deleted snapshots and does not reduce storage cost of a snapshot you intend to keep.

questions.question: An administrator accidentally deleted a production EBS snapshot yesterday. What should have been configured in advance to recover it?
options: A Recycle Bin rule retaining deleted snapshots for a chosen period between 1 day and 1 year
EBS Snapshot Archive on the snapshot with a 24 to 72 hour restore window
Fast Snapshot Restore on the volume that was restored from the snapshot
Delete on Termination disabled on the snapshot's source volume
questions.explanation: Recycle Bin for EBS Snapshots uses rules that retain deleted snapshots so they can be recovered, with a retention period from 1 day to 1 year, and the rules must be set up before the deletion. Archive is a cheaper storage tier, not an undelete mechanism; FSR addresses first-use latency of restored volumes; Delete on Termination governs volumes at instance termination, not snapshots.

questions.question: After restoring a volume from a snapshot, an application shows high latency on its first reads until the data is fully accessed. Which feature addresses this requirement?
options: EBS Snapshot Archive, which pre-loads the snapshot to the target AZ
Fast Snapshot Restore, which forces full initialization at extra cost
A Recycle Bin rule that keeps the snapshot for 1 year
Delete on Termination enabled on the restored volume
questions.explanation: Fast Snapshot Restore forces full initialization of the snapshot so the restored volume has no latency on first use, and it costs extra ($$$). Archive is a cheaper tier with a 24 to 72 hour restore and does not pre-load data; Recycle Bin only retains deleted snapshots; Delete on Termination has no effect on read latency.

questions.question: Which comparison between EBS Snapshot Archive and Fast Snapshot Restore is correct?
options: Archive reduces storage cost but slows restore; FSR removes first-use latency but increases cost
Archive removes first-use latency; FSR reduces storage cost by 75%
Both reduce cost, and both restore within 24 to 72 hours
Both require the volume to be detached before use
questions.explanation: Archive trades restore speed for cost (75% cheaper, restore within 24 to 72 hours), while FSR trades money for speed (full initialization, no first-use latency, extra cost) — they solve opposite problems. The roles are not reversed; neither option describes two cost reducers or a common 24 to 72 hour window; and detaching is not required for snapshots in either case, only recommended.
